questions.q: What is the single word Captain Hagberd repeats most often when referring to his son's return, and what does it signify about his perception of time?
questions.a: The word is "tomorrow." It signifies that Hagberd lives in a perpetual future that never becomes present; his madness consists of freezing time at the moment of hoped-for reunion, making "tomorrow" a shield against the reality that his son may never come. A wrong answer (e.g., "next month" or "soon") shows the student has not noticed the textual shift from "next month" to "tomorrow" and misses the central motif of the story.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Captain Hagberd wears a suit made of No. 1 sailcloth and tarred twine, and what this choice reveals about his identity.
questions.a: Hagberd wears the sailcloth suit because he made it himself "for the present" — a phrase he uses to deflect questions. The suit symbolizes his clinging to a sailor's identity even though he hated the sea; it is a uniform of his self-imposed isolation and a physical manifestation of his refusal to move on. A wrong answer that focuses only on the suit's oddness or material misses its psychological function as armor against a world that mocks him.

questions.q: Using the barber's narrative (pages 40-42), trace the sequence of events that led Hagberd to settle in Colebrook. Present it as a numbered timeline.
questions.a: 1. Hagberd's son Harry runs away to sea. 2. Hagberd's wife dies. 3. Hagberd receives a hoax letter suggesting Harry was seen near Colebrook. 4. Hagberd arrives in Colebrook in mourning, searches frantically. 5. He finds no trace, but cannot leave. 6. He buys land, builds cottages, and settles to wait. A student who omits the hoax letter or the wife's death fails to see the dual trauma (loss of wife + false hope) that triggers his delusion.

questions.q: Compare Captain Hagberd's relationship with Bessie Carvil to his relationship with the townspeople. What does the contrast reveal about his need for validation?
questions.a: With townspeople, Hagberd is secretive, miserly, and easily offended; he avoids them because their "grins" threaten his delusion. With Bessie, he talks "paternally, reasonably, and dogmatically," winks affectionately, and shares his plans — she is the sole witness who does not mock him. The contrast shows he craves an audience that accepts his reality; Bessie's silent compliance sustains his equilibrium. A weak answer merely states they are different without linking to his fragile self-esteem.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Captain Hagberd's madness is a rational response to an irrational world." Support your judgment with two pieces of evidence from the text.
questions.a: The statement is partially defensible: Hagberd constructs a coherent internal logic (advertising, preparing the house, setting a daily ritual) that gives him agency in a world where he lost his wife, his son, and his homeland. Evidence: (1) He reasons that since Harry once chose Colebrook, he will return there — a logical leap that becomes his anchor. (2) He stops offering rewards because he believes he has already "attained all that could be expected" — a twisted cost-benefit analysis. However, his violence toward the real Harry (throwing a shovel) shows the delusion has overtaken reason. A student who simply agrees or disagrees without textual evidence fails the evaluation task.

questions.q: Write a 100-word monologue from Captain Hagberd's perspective on the night before Harry's supposed return, capturing his voice, syntax, and the word "tomorrow" at least twice.
questions.a: A strong monologue uses Hagberd's repetitive, dogmatic tone: "Tomorrow he comes. Tomorrow the waiting ends. I have dug the garden, filled the cottage, bought the seeds — all for tomorrow. Bessie thinks I'm mad; the barber laughs. But I know. The sea cannot keep a Hagberd. We belong to the land, to the fireside. Tomorrow he will walk through that door, and I will say, 'You're home, Harry. You're home at last.' Tomorrow. Just tomorrow." A weak monologue uses modern language, lacks the "for the present" evasion, or misses the rhythmic certainty of "tomorrow."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the protagonist involves examining the central character's traits, motivations, conflicts, and development through textual evidence — appearance, dialogue, actions, inner thoughts, and ______ — to understand their role in advancing the story's themes.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you meet a neighbor who insists a long-lost relative will arrive "______" — every single day for years.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write a structured character analysis of Captain Hagberd using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) that covers his physical description, speech patterns, relationship with Bessie Carvil, the origin of his madness, and the symbolic significance of his "tomorrow," with at least three textual references.
